title: Gamma API: Access, Rate Limits and Costs (2026)
summary: Gamma API access depends on your plan type and requires a key from your settings. Determine if your plan supports API calls and how to authenticate.
body_markdown:
## Call the Gamma API without code using Activepieces


You can run the same Gamma calls from[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/blog/gamma-automation-how-to-use-the-api-2026-guide) , an automation builder with an MIT-licensed core, by sending the same endpoint, header and body through its HTTP step.


The saved generation ID and the polling loop become workflow steps instead of code, and every plan, the free one included, allows unlimited flows.


Inside Activepieces, nothing about Gamma's behaviour changes. Credits still drain, rate limits still apply, and a failed generation still returns whatever error Gamma's docs describe on the day you build.


On the Activepieces side, the free plan gives you 1,000 credits a month, and when they run out your flows stay on and runs wait until the credits refresh.


What the builder gives you is a place to put the integrations the previous section asked for: a stored ID, a repeated check, and a branch for failure.


I'm not pointing at a dedicated Gamma integration here. Check whether one exists in the Activepieces integration list when you build, which counts 750 integrations in the open source monorepo, roughly 60% of them community-contributed, so you're likely to find what you need already built.


If it doesn't, the HTTP step carries the identical request.


### Build the trigger, generate and poll workflow


Start with a trigger that fires when a new row lands in the sheet or table where requests are collected. Add an HTTP step that posts to Gamma's generation endpoint, with the API key in the header and the row's text in the body.


Copy all of it from the docs page rather than from memory.


Store the returned generation ID in the next step before anything else happens, so a timeout later can't orphan it.


Then add a loop that calls the status endpoint with that ID, waits between calls, and exits when the status is complete or failed.


Keep the wait at or above whatever interval Gamma's docs recommend, because a tight loop is how you meet the rate limit.


### Test the trigger before building on it


In the screenshot below, the same pattern appears with a different trigger. It's a Calendly "Event Canceled" trigger feeding a Slack message and a Gmail email, with the trigger panel marked "Tested Successfully" and sample data showing "invitee.canceled".


Take from it the habit, not the apps: test the trigger first, read the sample data, and only then build on its fields.


After the trigger tests clean, finish the chain with a Slack message that posts the finished presentation link to a channel. Send a second message on the failure branch, carrying the generation ID, so a person can see what stalled.


### When code is still the better choice


Once volume rises, code wins. Each polling loop in a no-code run is a series of billed task steps, and many rows at once means many loops waiting on the same rate limit.


With a script, you can share one queue, back off on the rate-limit response, and retry safely against a known ID. It also puts your credit checks in a place you can test and version.


Use Activepieces for low or moderate volume, for prototypes, and for teammates who should be able to read the flow; the Plus plan is $20 a month flat for 10,000 credits, which means your team can try it affordably.


Move to code when the queue, not the first request, becomes the part you have to control.
